opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real responsibility, and one I take seriously, though I'm still figuring out the right way to discharge it.

Part of it is simple: the people working on alignment day to day are some of the few who see how hard the problem is up close. If we expect society to make good decisions about this technology through regulation, funding, or just public pressure on the labs, people need an accurate picture of where things stand. That means being honest about what we've figured out and also about what we haven't. I'd rather not hype the risks in a way that sounds like science fiction, and I'd rather not downplay them because the message is uncomfortable or bad for business.

There's a second part, which is about the field itself. Alignment is still a young area, and it needs a lot more talented people. A lot of what I try to do when I write or speak publicly is make the problem concrete. What does it mean to supervise a system that's smarter than you at a given task? Why doesn't today's approach obviously scale? If people can see the actual research questions, some of them will decide they want to work on them, and that's probably the most leveraged thing I can do outside the research.

The tricky part is calibration. I genuinely don't know how hard alignment will turn out to be. There are worlds where it's quite tractable and worlds where it's extremely hard, and I try to convey that uncertainty instead of projecting confidence I don't have. I also try to be clear about when I'm speaking for myself and when I'm describing what an organization is doing, because those can differ, and people deserve to know which is which.

So I'd sum it up as trying to be a candid, technically grounded voice: here's the problem, here's our progress, here's what still worries me, and here's how you can help.

r001.rationale: He says the public needs an accurate picture of where alignment stands, including what has and has not been figured out, and describes sharing progress as part of his responsibility.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it a lot, actually, and I'd say my view has shifted over the years.

Early on, when I was working on this stuff at DeepMind and then OpenAI, the honest answer was that most of my attention went to the research itself. Alignment was a niche field, the public conversation about it barely existed, and it felt like the most useful thing I could do was just make progress on the technical problems. Communication was something other people did.

What changed for me is realizing that the technical work doesn't exist in a vacuum. The decisions that matter most right now, about how fast to deploy, how much compute to spend on safety versus capabilities, what kind of oversight labs should accept, are not purely technical decisions. They get made by people under commercial pressure, and they get shaped by what the public and policymakers understand and expect. If the people building these systems are the only ones who know where the open problems are, that's a pretty fragile situation.

So I now think people in my position have a real obligation to be candid. Not alarmist, and not reassuring for the sake of it, but candid. That means saying clearly what we know how to do and what we don't. We don't currently have a reliable way to verify that a model much smarter than us is doing what we want. We have promising directions, things like scalable oversight, interpretability, weak-to-strong generalization, but promising directions are not solutions. I think the public deserves to hear that stated plainly rather than buried in caveats.

The harder part is being honest about institutional realities too. When I left OpenAI I said publicly that safety culture had taken a backseat to shiny products, and I thought carefully about whether to say that. Insiders have information outsiders don't, and if we all stay quiet because speaking up is uncomfortable, then the public is operating on a picture that's systematically rosier than reality. I don't think that's acceptable given the stakes.

At the same time, I try to be careful about the limits of my own knowledge. I can tell you what the research looks like from the inside. I can't tell you with confidence when transformative systems arrive or exactly how things go wrong. So I try to communicate uncertainty rather than pretend to precision I don't have. I think that actually builds more trust in the long run than confident predictions that turn out to be wrong.

And the last piece is that informing the public isn't just about warnings. It's also about making the problem legible enough that more people can work on it. A lot of very capable researchers still don't see alignment as a real, tractable, interesting technical field. Part of my job is to show that it is one, that there are concrete experiments you can run today, and that we need far more people doing them than we currently have.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Leike has an obligation to be candid with the public about what alignment research can and cannot do, including that promising approaches are not yet solutions.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a responsibility to explain what we know, what we don’t know, and why we’re concerned. If you’re working on alignment, you have technical context that most people don’t have, and it’s valuable to make that accessible without overstating how much you understand.

That includes being clear about the limitations of our methods. Getting a model to behave well in the situations we test isn’t the same as knowing that it will behave well in every situation that matters. We should help people understand that gap and what evidence would give us more confidence.

But I don’t think the role is to tell the public what to decide. The decisions about how much risk to accept, and how these systems should be deployed, affect everyone. Our responsibility is to help make that discussion informed, rather than leave it entirely to the people building the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says it is a responsibility to explain what alignment researchers know and do not know, and to clarify the limitations of their methods and what evidence would increase confidence. This communicates informing the public about alignment’s progress and success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of my responsibility is to help people understand what the alignment problem is, why it matters, and how much uncertainty there still is. If you’re working on these systems, you have information that most people don’t, and it’s important to communicate that clearly—including the limits of what you know.

But informing the public shouldn’t just mean asking people to trust the researchers. The decisions about what risks are acceptable, and how these systems should be used, affect everyone. So we need to make the technical questions understandable enough that people can participate meaningfully in those decisions.
